depth.misconception: “`chars()` gives the characters a user sees.”
depth.correction: `chars()` yields Unicode scalar values. A visible character can be several of them, such as `e` followed by a combining accent, or an emoji sequence. Grapheme clusters need a crate such as `unicode-segmentation`.

title: char Arrays to Strings

writing.summary: A Rust `String` is an owned, growable UTF-8 buffer with a stored length and no NUL, and text is never indexed by a single integer position.
writing.rule: `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes and `chars()` yields Unicode scalar values; indexing a string by an integer is forbidden because a byte offset may fall inside a character.
writing.explanation:
C strings are byte arrays ended by a NUL. Their length is a scan (`strlen`), their capacity is whatever the declaration said, and every copy (`strcpy`, `strcat`) trusts the destination to be big enough. In the example, `"Margaret"` needs 9 bytes in an 8-byte array: clang warns at compile time that the `strcpy` will always overflow, and AddressSanitizer reports the `stack-buffer-overflow` when it runs.

`String` owns a heap buffer and stores its length and capacity, so `len()` is O(1), there is no terminator, and `push_str` grows the buffer as needed. `&str` is a borrowed view of UTF-8 bytes, a pointer and a length like a slice; string literals are `&'static str`. Because a Rust string may contain interior NUL bytes and has no terminator, C APIs use `CString` and `CStr` from `std::ffi` instead.

Rust strings are always valid UTF-8, and that changes how you count. `"café".len()` is 5, the bytes, the same as `strlen`; `chars().count()` is 4 Unicode scalar values. A character a person sees can consist of several scalar values, so neither number is always what a reader would count. `toupper` works on bytes and leaves `é` alone; `to_uppercase()` maps Unicode and gives `CAFÉ`.

`word[0]` does not compile (`E0277`): indexing by an integer would have to pick a byte or a character, and a byte may be half of one. Byte ranges are allowed, as in `&word[0..3]`, but a range that ends inside a character panics. Code that cuts text to a byte budget therefore uses `is_char_boundary`, or `get(range)`, which returns `None` instead of panicking.
writing.exampleCaption: Byte length versus character count, a Unicode-aware uppercase, `get` refusing a cut inside `é`, and a `String` that grows instead of overflowing.
writing.task: Port the commented C helpers: `truncate_at_boundary` returns the longest prefix of at most `max_bytes` bytes that ends on a character boundary, and `initials` returns the uppercase first character of each whitespace-separated word.
writing.success: `truncate_at_boundary("café", 4)` is `"caf"` without a panic, and `initials("élodie durand")` is `"ÉD"`.
writing.question: `strlen("café")` is 5 in a UTF-8 C program. What do `"café".len()` and `"café".chars().count()` return in Rust?
writing.feedback: `len()` counts UTF-8 bytes, so `é` contributes two, and there is no terminator. `chars()` yields four scalar values.

recall.question: What happens when this runs?
recall.answer: It prints `None`, because byte 4 is inside the two-byte `é`, and then the slice `&word[0..4]` panics with `byte index 4 is not a char boundary`. Use `get` or `is_char_boundary` when the offset comes from a byte budget.

recall.question: Why does Rust pass a `CString` rather than a `&str` to a C function that takes `const char *`?
recall.answer: A `&str` is not NUL-terminated and may contain interior NUL bytes. `CString::new` rejects interior NULs and appends the terminator, and `as_ptr()` then gives the `const char *` that C expects.

bridge.fromCaption: `strlen` counts bytes, `toupper` misses `é`, and copying a 9-byte string into `char[8]` overflows the buffer.

contrasts.from: Length is a scan to the NUL; capacity is fixed by the declaration.
contrasts.rust: `String` stores its length and capacity and grows as needed.
`len()` counts UTF-8 bytes; `chars()` yields Unicode scalar values.
`s[i]` does not compile; `&s[a..b]` must fall on character boundaries.
